claims.claim: Microsoft publishes Terms of Use for Web IQ: a customer needs an existing Microsoft Customer Agreement (an 'Enterprise Subscription'), must register each application with a description of its intended use, and may use the service only in applications Microsoft approves, under a limited, non-exclusive, non-transferable, revocable licence.

The Web IQ terms forbid using Web IQ content to train, evaluate or improve any LLM, forbid redistributing, reselling or sublicensing the service or content, forbid building a substitute or competing service with it, and bar copying, caching or databasing content except where the terms allow.
Under the Web IQ terms the customer, not Microsoft, pays any licensing or other fees owed to news publishers for displaying or using Web IQ responses, and must defend Microsoft against such claims.

For LLM use, the Web IQ terms require source attribution with a link near the LLM output, bar summaries that substitute for the grounding content, and cap verbatim grounding content shown from any one source at 200 characters, or less if the site owner sets a lower limit.

The Web IQ terms let a customer keep LLM summaries per end user in chat history for up to 30 days (unless refreshed); other storage of content is barred beyond transient processing within one request or workflow.

The Web IQ terms oblige customers to send Microsoft, through a real-time callback API, the result URLs used and acted on in each session, no later than 15 minutes after each response, starting within 60 days of the effective date; failure is a material breach.
Under the Web IQ terms Microsoft may end access if a customer does not fix the cause of a suspension within 60 days, or within 7 days for breaches of the LLM-use terms.

The Grounding with Bing terms for enterprise integrations such as Azure Foundry (a separate document, updated November 2025) let customers copy, store, cache or archive output only as an integrated part of their own work product, not as a substitute database, index or search offering; they also require Microsoft's references to be kept exactly as provided, bar using output to train, evaluate or improve AI models, and exclude the service from Microsoft's DPA.
Yahoo launched Scout, an AI assistant, in January 2026 (2026-01-27 per PPC Land's timeline), using Microsoft's Bing grounding API alongside Yahoo's own data.
Yahoo Search's organic results come from Microsoft's Bing: DuckDuckGo's 2021 white paper says Yahoo has bought its organic web links from Microsoft since 2009.

DuckDuckGo's white paper (March 2021) describes search syndication: engines such as Yahoo and DuckDuckGo buy organic links from Google or Microsoft, show that provider's search ads beside them, and split the ad revenue by contract percentages it does not disclose.
DuckDuckGo names Microsoft as its search-ads partner; clicks on Microsoft-provided ads pass through Microsoft Advertising. No price for organic Bing results is disclosed.

A March 2023 TechHQ report says DuckDuckGo, You.com and Neeva licensed Bing's index for their regular search, that Microsoft told at least two licensees that feeding Bing data to AI chat tools breached their contracts and might end their licences, and that Microsoft said it was working with out-of-compliance partners on a path forward; no prices or revenue shares are given.

OpenAI's help article on ChatGPT search for Enterprise and Edu says ChatGPT may send de-identified search queries to Bing to return web results, with requests sent on behalf of OpenAI and not tied to a customer or user account; ChatGPT for Healthcare workspaces don't use Bing.
SISTRIX, an SEO data vendor, says Perplexity uses the Bing index for current information; it gives no source, contract, terms, or share of Perplexity requests served by Bing.

Reuters (citing Bloomberg, 2026-01-29) reports a $750M, three-year Perplexity agreement to use Microsoft Azure and Foundry for access to OpenAI, Anthropic and xAI models; it describes no purchase of Bing web results.
Microsoft's FY2026 10-K (year to 2026-06-30) reports $24.1B of revenue from commercial arrangements with OpenAI, including revenue-sharing payments, with no Bing or search breakout.

Microsoft's FY2026 10-K says its Search advertising line covers Bing, Copilot, Microsoft News, Edge and third-party affiliates, and that it has several partnerships through which it provides and monetizes search; it names no partner and gives no terms.
Grounding with Bing Search and Grounding with Bing Custom Search are each listed at $14 per 1,000 transactions.
Both Grounding with Bing plans are capped at 150 transactions per second and 1 million transactions a day.

Grounding with Bing is an add-on usable only in Azure AI Foundry Agent Service or as Web Knowledge Source in Azure AI Search and Foundry Knowledge; outputs can't be used directly in other applications, cite the publishers, and are billed per grounding transaction.

The standard Grounding with Bing terms (November 2025) grant a limited, non-exclusive, non-transferable, revocable licence, require attribution, bar training AI models on output, and bar redistribution, resale, sublicensing and copying, caching or archiving output.
Web IQ is in limited access for select enterprise customers, with priority for organizations working with Microsoft account teams on production AI workloads.
Microsoft names Nasdaq (Nasdaq Boardvantage) as a Web IQ user; no price, volume or commitment is disclosed.
Microsoft says the infrastructure behind Web IQ already serves Copilot and OpenAI's ChatGPT (for some of ChatGPT's web answers) and other large AI platforms; no terms are disclosed.
OpenAI's ChatGPT search help says ChatGPT search sometimes sends rewritten queries to other search providers and points to Microsoft's and Shopify's privacy policies; it gives no commercial terms.

In September 2023 Meta and Microsoft announced that Meta AI (and other Meta AIs in WhatsApp, Messenger and Instagram) gets real-time search results through a partnership with Bing; neither announcement discloses price, revenue share or volume.
DuckDuckGo says its traditional links and images come largely from Bing, alongside its own crawler, indexes and specialist sources; it gives no share, fee or volume.
Microsoft retired the Bing Search APIs on 2025-08-11 and pointed customers to Grounding with Bing Search in Azure AI Agents.
Microsoft launched Web IQ on 2026-06-02 without a published price; no Web IQ price appears on Microsoft's pages as of 2026-09-27.

Microsoft positions Web IQ for agents and multi-step workflows, returning results directly to developers, while Grounding with Bing stays available to existing customers as an entry point inside Azure Foundry.
Perplexity says its Search API runs on the same infrastructure and its own index as its answer engine; the index tracks over 200 billion unique URLs. It makes no statement about buying Bing results.
Microsoft's 2026-04-27 post on the next phase of its OpenAI partnership covers cloud, IP licensing and revenue sharing, and says nothing about Bing or search pricing.

questions.notes: Status partial: named 2026 buyers are verified (OpenAI's ChatGPT, Nasdaq, Yahoo's Scout, DuckDuckGo; Meta only as of 2023), but no negotiated terms (price, revenue share, volume) exist for any of them. Two term documents change KB lines. First, Microsoft now has public Web IQ Terms of Use; the KB says none are published. They contain no price. Second, the Grounding with Bing terms the KB cites say they don't apply to Azure Foundry. The enterprise version that does apply allows storing output as part of the customer's own work product. The standard list terms ($14 per 1K, 150 TPS, 1M a day) are unchanged and known. Yahoo Scout on Bing's grounding API comes from PPC Land only (r18, r27). Perplexity's $750M deal is for Azure and Foundry model access, not Bing. SISTRIX's claim that Perplexity uses Bing is unsourced, and Perplexity says it runs its own index. Verdict policy: cids about Web IQ performance or coverage (latency, speed multiple, languages, verticals, test data centres, twenty years of Bing, content mix) and DuckDuckGo or Perplexity trivia are marked irrelevant when true. They name no buyer and no term. c65 is a negative research statement that its cited page can't state, so it's unsupported. Access: curl was blocked (403) for help.openai.com, perplexity.ai, techhq, neowin, windowsreport, reuters, searchengineland and SEW. Those were read in a browser, through WebFetch, or from Wayback captures (SEL 2026-08-23, Perplexity intro 2026-08-29, SEW 2026-09-01). The 10-K came from Wayback (2026-09-25). The malformed OpenAI help URL for c27 and c70 resolves to the article. r7 and r33 (Meta and Facebook pages) carry no claim. r2, r3, r8, r9, r11, r12, r13, r15, r20, r31 and r32 carry no buyer or term claims.

claims.claim: OpenAI prices the generally available web_search tool at $10.00 per 1,000 calls for all models, plus search content tokens billed at the chosen model's rates.
Image web search is priced the same: $10.00 per 1,000 calls plus search content tokens at model rates.

The legacy web_search_preview tool costs $10.00 per 1,000 calls plus content tokens at model rates on reasoning models (gpt-5, o-series), and $25.00 per 1,000 calls with free content tokens on non-reasoning models.
For gpt-4o-mini and gpt-4.1-mini with the non-preview tool, search content is billed as a fixed 8,000 input tokens per call.

OpenAI's pricing page lists gpt-5-search-api, the Chat Completions search model, at $1.25 per 1M input tokens, $0.125 per 1M cached input and $10 per 1M output tokens. The row sits in the collapsed 'Search' group of the specialized-models table.
At launch on 2025-03-11, OpenAI priced web search from $30 per 1,000 queries for GPT-4o search and $25 per 1,000 for GPT-4o mini search.

On 2025-06-26 OpenAI simplified web search pricing to $25 per 1,000 tool calls for the GPT-4o and GPT-4.1 series and $10 per 1,000 for o-series reasoning models. The changelog dates the change to 2025-06-24.
OpenAI priced its deep research API models by tokens: o3-deep-research at $10 per 1M input and $40 per 1M output, and o4-mini-deep-research at $2 and $8.
OpenAI shut down the o3-deep-research and o4-mini-deep-research models (2025-06-26 snapshots) on 2026-07-23, after announcing their deprecation on 2026-04-22. The listed substitute is gpt-5.6-sol.
The 2026-04-22 deprecation notice also covered gpt-4o-search-preview and gpt-4o-mini-search-preview, naming gpt-5.6-terra as their substitute.

gpt-4o-search-preview and gpt-4o-mini-search-preview shut down on 2026-07-23. The web_search_preview tool remains for legacy integrations, and OpenAI recommends web_search, or gpt-5-search-api for Chat Completions.
OpenAI's API changelog dates image results in web search to 2026-06-09.
OpenAI added return_token_budget to the web search tool on 2026-05-11, for longer GPT-5+ reasoning search runs. The guide warns it can raise latency and cost.
OpenAI's web search guide says each 'search' action incurs the tool-call charge. It lists open_page and find_in_page as other actions without stating a charge for them.
In an April 2025 community post, a developer relays OpenAI support saying one web search tool invocation can run several internal sub-searches, each billed as a separate call.
OpenAI's deep research guide offers max_tool_calls to cap the total tool calls (web search, MCP) in a deep research request, and calls it the primary lever on cost and latency.
A deep research request must include at least one data source: web search, remote MCP servers, or file search.
OpenAI says the Responses API isn't priced separately: tokens and tools are billed at standard rates, and tokens used by built-in tools are billed at the chosen model's rates.
OpenAI defines web search content tokens as tokens retrieved from the search index and fed to the model alongside the prompt.
On 2026-07-30 OpenAI cut GPT-5.6 Luna's API price by 80% (to $0.20/$1.20 per 1M tokens) and Terra's by 20% (to $2/$12). This lowers the content-token part of web search costs on those models.
TokenCost estimates that one o3 or o4-mini deep research query fires 10 to 30 web searches ($0.10 to $0.30 in search fees at $10 per 1,000), for about $1.45 per query on o3 or $0.41 on o4-mini.

Every OpenAI web search call is billed at $10 per 1,000 plus a fixed 8,000 input tokens. (False: the pricing page limits the fixed 8,000-token block to gpt-4o-mini and gpt-4.1-mini with the non-preview tool.)
OpenAI lists a generic built-in 'tool call' fee of $2.50 per 1,000 calls. (False: on the pricing page that row belongs to File search, whose tool-call pricing applies to the Responses API only.)
OpenAI added image results and return_token_budget to web search in July 2026. (False: the changelog dates them to 2026-06-09 and 2026-05-11.)

questions.notes: Status answered: the 2026 prices are pinned on OpenAI's pricing page ($10 per 1K plus content tokens for web_search and image search; preview tool $10 per 1K plus tokens on reasoning models and $25 per 1K with free tokens on non-reasoning models; a fixed 8,000-token block on gpt-4o-mini and gpt-4.1-mini), all already in the KB. New price facts: gpt-5-search-api at $1.25/$0.125/$10 per 1M tokens (in the collapsed Search group of the table), the 2025 launch and June 2025 price points, and deep research token prices. The biggest 2026 change is a KB correction: the deprecations page shows o3-deep-research and o4-mini-deep-research shut down on 2026-07-23 (announced 2026-04-22, replaced by gpt-5.6-sol). The KB leaf and OpenAI's deep research guide still present them as current, and the web search guide now points deep research to gpt-5.5 at high reasoning. Errors: c5 reads File search's $2.50 per 1K tool-call row as a generic fee. c18 puts the image-results and return_token_budget additions in July 2026. c25 is a negative research statement its page can't state. The G2 article (c1, c10, c33, r28) showed a blank bot-check page in the browser, returned 403 to curl and WebFetch, and has no Wayback copy, so it's unverifiable. The Getty SEC exhibit (c7) has no Wayback capture and SEC needs contact details, so it's unverifiable (and off-topic). Marked irrelevant: the Cloudflare crawl pilot, ChatGPT plan quotas, the paused $200 Pro sign-ups, and the ChatGPT deep research feature update (none are API web search charges). Among search results, r17 generalizes the 8,000-token block to every call (recorded as false). The pages behind r3 and r8 no longer show the excerpted web search lines. r10 is a user's unconfirmed billing complaint ($15 per 1K on gpt-4.1-mini), not recorded as a claim. openai.com and G2 returned 403 to curl. The openai.com pages were read in a browser; the Cloudflare release via Wayback (2026-07-09).

claims.claim: In Moz's test (published 2026-09-01), Gemini 3.5 Flash through the API rarely ran more than 1 to 2 grounding queries per prompt, often none, even at medium or higher thinking. Moz had to push it to 4 to 6. At about five queries per prompt, grounding cost Moz roughly $7 per 100 prompts at $14 per 1,000 queries.

Alphabet's Q4 2025 remarks (2026-02-04) say its first-party models such as Gemini process over 10B tokens a minute through customers' direct API use, up from 7B the quarter before, and that over 120,000 enterprises use Gemini. No grounding figure is given.
Alphabet reported over 16B tokens a minute of direct API use of its first-party models in Q1 2026 (60% above the prior quarter, per the release). No grounding figure is given.

On Alphabet's Q2 2025 call, Google said more than 85,000 enterprises (including LVMH, Salesforce and DBS Bank) build with Gemini, driving 35x year-over-year growth in Gemini usage. No grounding figure is given.

Statistics aggregators put Gemini API traffic at about 85B requests a month (January 2026, +142% on March 2025). Omnibound cites Alphabet's Q1 2026 release partly as its source, but that release doesn't contain the figure.
Gemini 3 grounding with Google Search includes 5,000 free grounding queries a month, shared across Gemini 3 models, then costs $14 per 1,000 queries on both the Gemini API and Agent Platform.
Billing for Gemini 3 grounding began on 2026-01-05; the Gemini API changelog announced it on 2025-12-05.

Grounding on Gemini 2.x includes 1,500 free grounded prompts a day (shared by 2.0 Flash, 2.5 Flash and Flash-Lite; 10,000 a day for 2.5 Pro on Agent Platform), then $35 per 1,000 grounded prompts, one charge per prompt.
At launch on 2024-10-31, Grounding with Google Search on the paid Gemini API tier cost $35 per 1,000 grounded queries.
Gemini 3 bills each search query the model runs, so one prompt can bill several (empty queries are ignored); Gemini 2.5 and older bill once per grounded prompt.
Grounding with Google Search on Agent Platform has a documented limit of 1 million queries a day (more on request). It's a capacity cap, not a usage figure.
Agent Platform bills grounding only when a response returns at least one web source; on Gemini 3, input tokens supplied by grounding aren't charged, while model usage is billed separately.

questions.notes: Status unanswered: no pool item discloses or credibly reports how many queries Grounding with Google Search serves, or how fast that grows. Every price, allowance and limit in the pool is already in the KB. The 1M-a-day limit is a cap, not traffic. The nearest usage evidence is Gemini-wide, not grounding. Direct-API throughput went from 7B to 10B tokens a minute (Q4 2025) and then 16B (Q1 2026; carried by r30 and confirmed in Alphabet's Q1 2026 release via Wayback). Q2 2025 showed 35x growth in Gemini usage. Moz's test gives the one grounding-specific ratio: 1 to 2 queries per prompt on Gemini 3.5 Flash through the API. It bears on converting prompts to billable queries but doesn't pin volume. The 85B-requests-a-month figure appears only in statistics aggregators. c28 is unsupported: it says 5,000 free prompts a month, while its page (Parallel) says 5,000 queries, and Gemini 3 bills per query. c22 over-generalizes the 1,500-a-day allowance to all Gemini 2.5 models (2.5 Pro gets 10,000 on Agent Platform), but its figures match the page. Marked irrelevant when true, since they bear on neither volume nor the line's arithmetic: display rules, the Web Grounding for Enterprise index, API metadata, Cloud Next use cases and data partners, AI Overviews query growth, Gemini Enterprise interactions, and named Gemini customers. Access: ai.google.dev redirects to an auto sign-in check, which a cookie jar passes without logging in. abc.xyz returned 403 and was read from Wayback. Search results r1, r5, r9, r11 to r16, r19 to r22, r28, r29, r32 and r33 carry no grounding volume claim.
